nodes.label: Heraclius
nodes.full: Heraclius, who had destroyed the Persian empire's army in 627–628 and had restored the True Cross to Jerusalem in March 630, saw the Arab armies take Syria, Palestine and Egypt in the last years of his life; the emperor, in his sixties and ill, was unable to reverse the defeat at Yarmuk, and he died in February 641 leaving a divided succession and a state that had lost its richest provinces.
nodes.src: Walter Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003); Theophanes, Chronographia AM 6122–6132; John Haldon, Byzantium in the Seventh Century (1990).

nodes.label: Constans II
nodes.full: Constans II, who came to the throne at 11 in 641, held the empire through the Arab conquest of Egypt and North Africa and the naval defeat of the Battle of the Masts in 655, had his brother Theodosius killed, issued the Typos in 648 to quell the controversy over the divine and human wills of Christ and moved with the court to Syracuse in 662–663, where he was murdered in his bath in 668.
nodes.src: Haldon 1990; Theophanes AM 6133–6160; Kaegi 1992.

nodes.label: Constantine IV
nodes.full: Constantine IV defeated the first Arab siege of Constantinople of 674–678 with the use of Greek fire, made a thirty years' peace with Mu'awiya, summoned the Sixth Ecumenical Council of 680–681, which condemned Monotheletism, and failed to destroy the Bulgar state of Asparuh south of the Danube in 680–681, an event that made a new power in the Balkans.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6165–6177; Haldon 1990; Acts of the Sixth Council (680–681).

nodes.label: Justinian II
nodes.full: Justinian II, who made a treaty with Abd al-Malik, moved thousands of Slavs to Anatolia and lost them at Sebastopolis in 692, held the Quinisext Council of 692 and was overthrown in 695, had his nose cut off and was exiled to Cherson; he returned in 705 with Bulgar help, took revenge on his enemies in a reign of terror and was killed in 711, ending the Heraclian dynasty.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6177–6203; Nikephoros, Breviarium; Constance Head, Justinian II (1972).

nodes.label: Leo III
nodes.full: Leo, a general of the Anatolikon theme who took the throne in March 717 after years of anarchy, defeated the Arab siege of 717–718, repulsed the Arab armies in Anatolia at Akroinon in 740, issued with his son the Ecloga, a law code, in 741 and, from 726 or 730, began the policy of removing images from churches that is called Iconoclasm; he founded the dynasty that held the throne until 802.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6209–6232; Leslie Brubaker and John Haldon, Byzantium in the Iconoclast Era (2011); Haldon 1990.

nodes.label: Constantine V
nodes.full: Constantine V, after defeating his brother-in-law Artabasdos in 741–743, was an effective soldier who led nine campaigns against the Bulgars, repopulated Thrace with Syrians and Armenians, repaired the aqueduct of Valens after the plague and earthquake, made Iconoclasm the official doctrine by the council of Hieria of 754 and persecuted monks; his iconodule opponents gave him the name Kopronymos, dung-named.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6233–6267; Brubaker and Haldon 2011; Treadgold 1988.

nodes.label: Irene
nodes.full: Irene, widow of Leo IV and regent for her son Constantine VI from 780, summoned the Second Council of Nicaea in 787, which restored images, and in 797 had her son blinded in the room where he was born and ruled alone as emperor, the first woman to do so in her own name; she was deposed by the logothete Nikephoros in October 802 and died in exile on Lesbos in 803.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6272–6295; Judith Herrin, Women in Purple (2001); Lynda Garland, Byzantine Empresses (1999).

nodes.label: Nikephoros I
nodes.full: Nikephoros, Irene's finance minister, carried out a fiscal reform, resettled farmers in the Balkans, took taxes from monasteries and the church and, in 811, led a great expedition against the Bulgar khan Krum, sacked the capital Pliska and was killed in a Bulgar ambush on 26 July, the first emperor to die in battle since 378; Krum made a drinking cup of his skull.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6295–6303; Warren Treadgold, The Byzantine Revival 780–842 (1988).

nodes.label: Theophilos
nodes.full: Theophilos, a learned and just emperor of the Amorian house founded by Michael II, who had come to power after the revolt of Thomas the Slav, built the Sea Walls of the city, fought the caliph al-Mu'tasim, who in 838 took Amorion in the heart of Anatolia, and held to Iconoclasm; he was called by the people the Just for his sitting in judgement, and died in 842 leaving his wife Theodora as regent for his young son.
nodes.src: Treadgold 1988; Genesios; Theophanes Continuatus; Brubaker and Haldon 2011.

nodes.label: Theodora, Michael III and Bardas
nodes.full: Theodora, regent for the child Michael III from 842, ended Iconoclasm in 843, was removed in 856 by her brother Bardas, who became the effective ruler and patron of learning; Michael III, who took pleasure in horse races and drinking, made Basil the Macedonian his colleague and was murdered by Basil in September 867, ending the Amorian dynasty and opening the Macedonian.
nodes.src: Theophanes Continuatus; Genesios; Treadgold 1988; Garland 1999.

nodes.label: Yarmuk
nodes.full: After weeks of manoeuvre in the gorge of the Yarmuk river the Byzantine army, under the generals Theodore Trithyrios and Vahan, and with many Armenian and Ghassanid troops, was routed in August 636 by Khalid ibn al-Walid's Arab cavalry, with a large part destroyed in the river valley; the defeat ended Byzantine rule in Syria, where Damascus had already fallen, and Heraclius is said to have remarked: farewell, Syria.
nodes.src: Al-Tabari, History; Theophanes AM 6126; Walter Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992).

nodes.label: Jerusalem and Egypt lost
nodes.full: Jerusalem surrendered to the caliph Umar after a siege in 637–638, Caesarea in 640, and the Arab army under Amr ibn al-As took Egypt from 639, defeating the Byzantine force at Heliopolis in 640 and taking Alexandria in 642; the city was briefly recovered in 645 and the coastal cities of Syria fell by 640, so that within a decade the empire had lost its richest provinces and the grain supply of Constantinople.
nodes.src: John of Nikiu, Chronicle; Kaegi 1992; Hugh Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007).

nodes.label: First Arab siege
nodes.full: The Arab fleet of Mu'awiya, which had won the battle of the Masts in 655 and taken Rhodes and Cyzicus as bases, besieged the city by sea in the summers of 674 to 678; Constantine IV's ships, equipped with Greek fire, burned the Arab fleet, a storm destroyed it on its way home, and the caliph made a peace for thirty years with an annual payment.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6165–6170; Kaegi 1992; John Haldon and Hugh Kennedy, ‘The Arab–Byzantine Frontier’, Zbornik radova 19 (1980).

nodes.label: Siege of 717–718
nodes.full: Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik's army and fleet, perhaps 80,000 men on 1,800 ships by the Arab sources, besieged the city for a year, but Leo III's diplomacy with the Bulgar khan Tervel, a severe winter, famine and plague in the camp, the Greek fire and the Byzantine victory over the second fleet broke the siege; the failure ended Arab hopes of taking the city and made Leo a hero.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6209; Brubaker and Haldon 2011; Marius Canard, ‘Les expéditions des Arabes contre Constantinople’, Journal asiatique 208 (1926).

nodes.label: Akroinon
nodes.full: In 740 Leo III and his son Constantine met an Arab army in Phrygia at Akroinon and won a victory that ended the large-scale invasions of the Arab raiders; the frontier along the Taurus became a zone of annual raids from both sides, with the Arab expeditions of the summer (sa'ifa) and the Byzantine themes' defences by forts and mountain passes.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6232; Michael Bonner, Aristocratic Violence and Holy War (1996); Haldon 1990.

nodes.label: Bulgars of Asparuh and Krum
nodes.full: The Bulgars of khan Asparuh crossed the Danube in 680–681 and founded a state in the plains and mountains of the later Bulgaria, which was recognised in a treaty by Constantine IV and became the empire's chief neighbour in Europe; under Krum (803–814) they took Serdica in 809, defeated and killed Nikephoros in 811, defeated Michael I at Versinikia in 813 and was preparing to besiege Constantinople before his sudden death in April 814.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6171–6305; John Fine, The Early Medieval Balkans (1983); Steven Runciman, A History of the First Bulgarian Empire (1930).

nodes.label: Amorion
nodes.full: After Theophilos had raided Syria and taken Zapetra, the caliph al-Mu'tasim led a great army into Anatolia, defeated the emperor at Dazimon and took Amorion, the home town of the dynasty, in August 838 after a siege of two weeks that was ended when a traitor showed a weak point in the wall; a large part of the garrison and population were killed or enslaved, and the event shocked the empire and was the subject of Abu Tammam's poem.
nodes.src: Al-Tabari, History; Treadgold 1988; Abu Tammam, Ode on Amorion; Genesios.

nodes.label: Crete and Sicily
nodes.full: Andalusi Muslim exiles from Cordoba took Crete in about 824–827 and founded an emirate that raided the Aegean for over a century; the Aghlabid emirs of Ifriqiya, invited by a rebel Byzantine governor, landed in Sicily in 827 and conquered Palermo in 831, Messina in 842, Syracuse in 878 and Taormina in 902, and the island was lost over seventy-five years.
nodes.src: Vasiliev, Byzance et les Arabes vol. 1 (1935); Alex Metcalfe, The Muslims of Medieval Italy (2009); Treadgold 1988.

nodes.label: Rus raid and Lalakaon
nodes.full: While Michael III's army was on the eastern frontier, a fleet of some 200 Rus ships appeared in June 860 at Constantinople, plundered the suburbs and went away after a few days, a first sign of a new power in the north that Patriarch Photios described in his homilies; in 863 the army of Petronas defeated and killed the emir of Melitene, Umar, at Lalakaon, a victory that began a Byzantine recovery.
nodes.src: Photios, Homilies 3–4; Genesios; Theophanes Continuatus; Treadgold 1988.

nodes.label: Thomas the Slav
nodes.full: Thomas, a soldier of Slavic origin who claimed to be Constantine VI, rose against Michael II in 821 with the thematic armies of the east, with the backing of the caliph, who crowned him, and a large following of the poor and Slavs and Armenians; he besieged Constantinople for a year and was defeated with Bulgar help by the Amorian emperor, in a civil war that is the largest of the century.
nodes.src: Genesios; Theophanes Continuatus; Treadgold 1988; Brubaker and Haldon 2011.

nodes.label: Fall of Ravenna
nodes.full: The Lombard king Aistulf took Ravenna, the seat of the exarch, the emperor's representative in Italy, in 751; the pope, unable to count on Constantinople, turned to the Franks and anointed Pepin in 754, and Pepin's gift of the exarchate to the pope in 756 created the Papal State and marked the end of the empire's rule in central and northern Italy.
nodes.src: Liber Pontificalis, Life of Stephen II; Thomas Brown, Gentlemen and Officers (1984); Judith Herrin, The Formation of Christendom (1987).

nodes.label: Themes
nodes.full: The field armies that had retreated from Syria and Egypt were settled in Anatolia in regions called themes (Anatolikon, Armeniakon, Opsikion, Thrakesion) under a general (strategos) who held both military and civil powers; soldiers received land or revenue in return for service, and the system, whose date and form are disputed by historians, was in place by the late seventh century and made the empire's army a provincial one.
nodes.src: Haldon 1990; Warren Treadgold, Byzantium and Its Army 284–1081 (1995); John Haldon, Warfare, State and Society in the Byzantine World (1999).

nodes.label: Ecloga
nodes.full: The Ecloga (Selection), issued by Leo III and Constantine V, was a short handbook in Greek of Justinian's law with changes concerning marriage, inheritance and punishment, including mutilation in place of death for many crimes; it was written for practical use in the courts and became the basis of later codes among the Slavs.
nodes.src: Ecloga (ed. Burgmann, 1983); Haldon 1990; Brubaker and Haldon 2011.

nodes.label: Farmer’s Law
nodes.full: The Nomos Georgikos, a brief set of rules on village life, probably of the late seventh or eighth century, deals with the fields, the herds, the vineyards and the shepherds, with penalties for theft and damage and with the rights of the village community; it reflects a world of free peasants working small farms in a time of cities in decline.
nodes.src: Nomos Georgikos (ed. Ashburner, 1910–1912); Haldon 1990; Ostrogorsky, History of the Byzantine State (1969).

nodes.label: Fiscal measures of Nikephoros
nodes.full: Nikephoros I, a former finance official, took a series of measures: higher taxes on land and on the churches and monasteries, new levies on the transfers of property, the enforced settlement of soldiers and peasants in the Balkans and the obligation of a village to pay the taxes of its defaulters (the allelengyon); his critics, Theophanes and the monks, called them the ten vexations.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6295; Treadgold 1988; Ostrogorsky 1969.

nodes.label: Charlemagne and two emperors
nodes.full: On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor of the Romans in St Peter's, which the Byzantine court, where Irene sat as sole empress, regarded as a usurpation; after years of dispute, Michael I's ambassadors in 812 addressed Charlemagne as basileus though not as emperor of the Romans, and the Latin West had a rival to the claim of the imperial title.
nodes.src: Royal Frankish Annals (800, 812); Herrin 1987; Theophanes AM 6293.

nodes.label: Monotheletism and Maximus
nodes.full: Heraclius' Ecthesis of 638, issued with Patriarch Sergius to heal the division with the Monophysites of Syria and Egypt, taught that Christ had one will; it was opposed by Pope Martin I and by Maximus the Confessor, whom Constans II had arrested in 653–655, tried and, in 662, mutilated and exiled to die in the Caucasus, and the doctrine was condemned at the Sixth Council of 680–681.
nodes.src: Ecthesis (638); Typos (648); Acts of the Lateran Council (649); Sixth Council (680–681); Pauline Allen and Bronwen Neil, Maximus the Confessor and His Companions (2002).

nodes.label: Iconoclasm
nodes.full: Whether the emperor Leo III issued a formal decree against images in 726 or 730 is disputed, but by about 730 the removal of the image of Christ from the Chalke Gate was a conflict over images in churches, on which Patriarch Germanos resigned; Constantine V's council at Hieria of 754 declared images idolatrous, and monks, who defended them as aids to the incarnation, were persecuted, blinded or exiled, with Stephen the Younger killed by a mob in 765.
nodes.src: Brubaker and Haldon 2011; Theophanes AM 6218; Council of Hieria (754); Stephen the Deacon, Life of Stephen the Younger.

nodes.label: Nicaea II
nodes.full: The council summoned by the regent Irene and the patriarch Tarasios, with some 350 bishops and delegates of the pope, restored the veneration of images, distinguishing a relative veneration (proskynesis) of images from the worship due to God alone; it was recognised as the Seventh Ecumenical Council, though a second period of Iconoclasm under Leo V in 815 reversed it.
nodes.src: Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea (787); Brubaker and Haldon 2011; Herrin 1987.

nodes.label: Triumph of Orthodoxy
nodes.full: After Theophilos' death the regent Theodora and the minister Theoktistos, with Patriarch Methodios, restored the images in a synod and a procession on the first Sunday of Lent, 11 March 843; the Synodikon of Orthodoxy that was read thereafter every year at that date condemned Iconoclasts by name, and the feast of the Triumph of Orthodoxy is still kept in the Orthodox churches.
nodes.src: Synodikon of Orthodoxy (843); Theophanes Continuatus; Brubaker and Haldon 2011.

nodes.label: Photios and the schism
nodes.full: The deposition of Patriarch Ignatios by Bardas and the appointment of the layman Photios, a scholar, in 858 divided the clergy; Pope Nicholas I rejected Photios, and the dispute over the jurisdiction of Bulgaria and the Frankish missionaries' addition of the filioque in the creed led in 867 to a council at Constantinople in which Photios deposed the pope, the first formal break between East and West.
nodes.src: Photios, Letters; Liber Pontificalis; Francis Dvornik, The Photian Schism (1948).

nodes.label: Cyril and Methodios
nodes.full: At the request of Prince Rastislav of Moravia, Michael III sent in 863 the brothers Constantine (Cyril) and Methodios of Thessalonica, who had invented an alphabet (Glagolitic) and translated the liturgy and scripture into Slavic; the Slavonic liturgy was approved by Pope Hadrian II in 869, and the work was later the base of the Slavic literatures.
nodes.src: Life of Constantine; Life of Methodios; Dvornik 1948; Dimitri Obolensky, The Byzantine Commonwealth (1971).

nodes.label: Paulicians
nodes.full: The Paulicians, a dualist and adoptionist sect, rejected icons, the cross and the Old Testament, lived in the Armenian highlands and in the east of Anatolia and, persecuted by Michael I, Leo V and Theodora, in the 840s moved to the frontier with the Arabs, where under their leader Karbeas they founded a base at Tephrike and fought as allies of the emirs.
nodes.src: Peter of Sicily, History of the Paulicians; Nina Garsoïan, The Paulician Heresy (1967).

nodes.label: Cross of Hagia Eirene
nodes.full: In the apse of the church of Hagia Eirene, rebuilt after the earthquake of 740 by Constantine V, a plain black mosaic cross on a gold ground replaced the figural images; the cross, with its inscription of the Psalm text on the arch, is the best-preserved large work of Iconoclast decoration in the city.
nodes.src: Cyril Mango, Byzantine Architecture (1976); Brubaker and Haldon 2011.

nodes.label: Chludov Psalter
nodes.full: The marginal Psalter now in the Historical Museum in Moscow, written in a small script and illustrated in the margins with scenes that make topical points, includes a famous illustration of the soldier who offers vinegar to Christ on the cross and of the iconoclast patriarch John the Grammarian whitewashing an icon, as an expression of the iconophile triumph.
nodes.src: Chludov Psalter (Moscow, State Historical Museum, MS gr. 129d); Kurt Weitzmann; Brubaker and Haldon 2011.

nodes.label: Kassia
nodes.full: Kassia (Kassiani), a nun and abbess from an aristocratic family, whom tradition says was a participant in the bride-show for Theophilos in 830 and lost the contest by a clever retort, composed some fifty hymns and over two hundred verses of epigrams, and her hymn on the woman who fell, sung in the Orthodox Church on Holy Wednesday, is one of the best-known works of Byzantine hymnography.
nodes.src: Antonía Tripolitis, Kassia: The Legend, the Woman, and Her Work (1992); Diane Touliatos-Miles.

nodes.label: Virgin of Hagia Sophia
nodes.full: On Holy Saturday 29 March 867 Patriarch Photios inaugurated the new mosaic of the Virgin and Child in the apse of Hagia Sophia, the first great image of the post-Iconoclast period, and in a homily proclaimed that the images, which the previous generation had removed, had now been restored to the heart of the church.
nodes.src: Photios, Homily 17; Cyril Mango, The Homilies of Photius (1958); Brubaker and Haldon 2011.

nodes.label: Theophanes’ Chronographia
nodes.full: Theophanes the Confessor (c. 760–818), a monk at the monastery of Megas Agros, completed in 814 the Chronographia, a year-by-year history from 284 to 813 that continued George Synkellos's chronicle and is the principal source for the seventh and eighth centuries; its strong iconophile bias and use of lost sources, among them eastern chronicles, are the subject of debate.
nodes.src: Theophanes, Chronographia (trans. Mango and Scott, 1997); Brubaker and Haldon 2011.

nodes.label: John of Damascus
nodes.full: John of Damascus, a monk in the monastery of Mar Saba in Palestine under Muslim rule and thus out of reach of the emperor, wrote three treatises in defence of images in about 730, in which he argued that since God had become matter in Christ, matter could be a means of grace; his arguments were taken up at Nicaea in 787.
nodes.src: John of Damascus, Three Treatises on the Divine Images (trans. Andrew Louth, 2003); Brubaker and Haldon 2011.

nodes.label: Leo the Mathematician
nodes.full: Leo the Mathematician, a teacher of Constantinople who studied in Andros and was said to have been put in charge of a school at the Magnaura palace by Bardas in the 850s, restored the teaching of Greek philosophy, geometry and astronomy; a manuscript copy of Euclid and Ptolemy was made in his circle, and he is credited with a device for signalling and with the throne of Solomon.
nodes.src: Theophanes Continuatus; Paul Lemerle, Byzantine Humanism (1986); Treadgold, The Nature of the Bibliotheca of Photius (1980).

nodes.label: Bibliotheca of Photios
nodes.full: Photios compiled, as he says for his brother, a collection of notices of 279 books read in his reading circle before his embassy, with summaries and extracts, an important source for many lost works of antiquity; in his homilies, letters and Amphilochia he laid out a theological and philological programme that made him a central figure of the ninth-century revival.
nodes.src: Photios, Bibliotheca (trans. N. G. Wilson, 1994); Lemerle 1986; Treadgold 1980.

nodes.label: Revival of learning
nodes.full: Under Bardas, Greek manuscripts began to be copied in the new minuscule script, ancient authors were studied again after a long gap, and Patriarch Photios and his circle collected and taught the classics; the revival has been called the first Byzantine humanism, and it prepared the encyclopaedic works of the tenth century.
nodes.src: Lemerle 1986; Nigel Wilson, Scholars of Byzantium (1983); Treadgold 1988.

nodes.label: Coinage and shrunken cities
nodes.full: The solidus remained the standard gold coin, but many provincial mints closed and the coins found in the cities of the empire's interior are few; archaeology shows that towns like Ephesus, Sardis and Corinth shrank to small fortified nuclei in the seventh century and that Constantinople itself fell from several hundred thousand people to perhaps 40,000 to 70,000.
nodes.src: Cécile Morrisson (ed.), Trade and Markets in Byzantium (2012); Michael Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985); Haldon 1990.

nodes.label: Free villages and Black Sea trade
nodes.full: The Farmer's Law and the evidence of villages point to a countryside of free smallholders with a village tax, while trade went on along the Black Sea between Cherson and the Khazar and Rus markets, in furs, wax, slaves and fish, and along the Aegean in the grain and oil of the islands; the markets of Constantinople were under the Eparch's supervision.
nodes.src: Haldon 1990; Hendy 1985; Book of the Eparch (10th c.).

nodes.label: Silk workshops
nodes.full: The silk industry, established under Justinian on the basis of the smuggled cocoons, continued in the state workshops that made cloth for the palace, diplomatic gifts and the church, with rich purple silks of Constantinople found in tombs and reliquaries in the West; the sale of the best silks was restricted and the export of the purple forbidden.
nodes.src: Anna Muthesius, Byzantine Silk Weaving (1997); Hendy 1985.

nodes.label: Greek fire
nodes.full: A liquid incendiary weapon, said to have been brought to Constantinople about 672 by Kallinikos, an architect from Heliopolis in Syria, was projected through siphons from the prows of the ships and burned on water; it was a state secret, whose composition (probably of petroleum with resins) is not known, and it won the battles of 674–678 and 717–718.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6163; John Haldon and Maurice Byrne, ‘A Possible Solution to the Problem of Greek Fire’, Byzantinische Zeitschrift 70 (1977); John Haldon, ‘“Greek Fire” Revisited’ (2006).

nodes.label: Walls and cisterns
nodes.full: After the plague of 747 and the empire's depopulation, Constantine V repaired the aqueduct of Valens in 766 by bringing in builders from Greece and Asia Minor, and the city's open cisterns were kept up; Theophilos rebuilt the sea walls and the land walls, with their inscriptions, in 829–842, a work against the Arab and Rus fleets.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6258; Cyril Mango, Le développement urbain de Constantinople (1985); Brubaker and Haldon 2011.

nodes.label: Beacons and automata
nodes.full: A chain of beacon fires from Loulon in the Taurus to the lighthouse in the palace passed news of Arab raids to the capital in an hour, an arrangement attributed to Leo the Mathematician; in the palace the throne of Solomon, with gilded lions and birds that sang and roared, was built under Theophilos and amazed the foreign envoys.
nodes.src: Constantine Porphyrogenitus, De ceremoniis; Liudprand, Antapodosis; Haldon, Warfare, State and Society (1999).

nodes.label: Khazar alliance
nodes.full: The Turkic Khazars north of the Caucasus helped Heraclius against Persia in 626–628 and later served as a barrier to the Arabs; Justinian II married the khagan's sister, who took the name Theodora, in 703–704, and in 769 Constantine V married his son Leo IV to Tzitzak, a Khazar princess, who took the name Irene and was the mother of Constantine VI; Leo IV himself was nicknamed the Khazar.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6169, 6261; Peter Golden, Khazar Studies (1980); Dunlop, The History of the Jewish Khazars (1954).

nodes.label: Rome, Franks and papacy
nodes.full: The popes, whose lands in Italy the empire could not defend against the Lombards and who rejected Iconoclasm, withdrew from the empire's authority in practice after 732; Leo III transferred in 732–733 southern Italy and Illyricum from the patriarch of Rome to Constantinople, and Pope Stephen II, after seeking help from Constantine V, went to Pepin, a turn that made the Frankish kingdom the papacy's protector.
nodes.src: Liber Pontificalis; Herrin 1987; Brown 1984.

nodes.label: Harun al-Rashid and prisoner exchanges
nodes.full: After the raids of 782 and 806 on Anatolia by Harun al-Rashid and the peace imposed on Irene and Nikephoros, with the payment of tribute, prisoners were exchanged in a sequence of exchanges on the Lamos river in Cilicia, of which the best recorded of 845 returned thousands of captives; the exchange was a regular diplomatic institution of the frontier.
nodes.src: Al-Tabari, History; Theophanes AM 6274, 6298; Vasiliev 1935.

nodes.label: Bulgar treaties
nodes.full: Treaties with the Bulgars in 716 under Tervel, in 815–816 under Omurtag, set the frontier in Thrace and provided for the exchange of prisoners and trade, and the khans' inscriptions in Greek from Pliska show that the Bulgar court used the language of Byzantium; the treaty of 816 was for thirty years.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6208; Pliska inscriptions; Fine 1983; Runciman 1930.

nodes.label: First Rus embassies
nodes.full: The Annals of St Bertin record that in 839 an embassy of Theophilos at the Frankish court at Ingelheim included men who called themselves Rhos, probably Scandinavians in Rus service, and who could not return by the Khazar route; after the attack of 860 the patriarch's circle described the Rus as a new people, and the baptism of some Rus was recorded in 860–867.
nodes.src: Annals of St Bertin (839); Photios, Letters; Obolensky 1971.

nodes.label: Plague and earthquake
nodes.full: The last wave of the plague that began in 541 reached Constantinople in 746–747 and, according to Theophanes, killed so many that the emperor had to bring settlers from Greece; the earthquake of 26 October 740 had damaged the walls and churches of the capital, and the two were followed by the resettlement of Thrace and the repair of the aqueduct.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6238, 6238–6239; Peter Sarris and Lester Little (eds.), Plague and the End of Antiquity (2007); Mango 1985.

nodes.label: Slavs in Greece
nodes.full: Slavic groups settled in the Balkans from the late sixth century, and by the 7th–8th centuries held much of Macedonia, Thessaly and the Peloponnese, whose population the Chronicle of Monemvasia says was for two centuries Slavic; the empire reconquered Greece in the late eighth and ninth centuries and settled Greek and Armenian colonists, and Hellenised the Slavs by the church and the army.
nodes.src: Chronicle of Monemvasia; Fine 1983; Florin Curta, The Making of the Slavs (2001).

nodes.label: Resettlement
nodes.full: Emperors moved peoples to change the balance of the provinces: Justinian II moved some 30,000 Slavs to Anatolia in 688–689, and Constantine V settled Syrians and Armenians from Melitene and Theodosiopolis in Thrace in 755–756 and again in 762, forming populations of Paulicians and Monophysites in Europe.
nodes.src: Theophanes AM 6180, 6247; Haldon 1990; Garsoïan 1967.

nodes.label: Empresses
nodes.full: Irene, Theodora wife of Theophilos and her successors as regents ruled as guardians of boys, and in Irene's case as sole ruler; the bride-shows by which the wives of emperors were chosen from daughters of provincial families, as for Theophilos and Constantine VI, are the best-known feature of the court, and the empress Theodora's role in the restoration of the icons gave her a saint's cult.
nodes.src: Herrin, Women in Purple (2001); Garland 1999; Treadgold 1988.

nodes.label: Thematic soldier
nodes.full: The stratiotes, a farmer-soldier with holdings in his village, served in the thematic army at his own cost as an armed horseman or infantryman, with a minimum of land that could not be alienated, and received a share of booty; the Life of St Philaretos the Merciful, a work of the early ninth century, gives a picture of a prosperous village notable in Paphlagonia, his ruin by raids and the rise of his granddaughter Maria to be empress.
nodes.src: Life of Philaretos (ed. Rydén, 2002); Haldon 1990; Treadgold 1995.

nodes.label: Jews and forced baptism
nodes.full: Heraclius ordered in about 632 that Jews of the empire be baptised, and Leo III in 721–722 is said by sources hostile to him to have issued a similar decree; the extent and enforcement of these orders are uncertain, and Jewish communities survived in Constantinople, Thessalonica, Southern Italy and Greece in the following centuries.
nodes.src: Doctrina Jacobi (c. 634); Nicholas de Lange (ed.), Greek Jewish Texts from the Cairo Genizah (1996); Andrew Sharf, Byzantine Jewry (1971).

nodes.label: Monks of Stoudios
nodes.full: The monastery of Stoudios under Theodore the Studite (759–826) became the most important monastic community of the capital, with a written rule, a scriptorium and a body of some 700 monks; Theodore's letters and his writings against Iconoclasm, written from exile in Anatolia, show the resistance of the monks to the emperors and the patriarchate.
nodes.src: Theodore the Studite, Letters (ed. Fatouros, 1992); Treadgold 1988; Thomas Pratsch, Theodoros Studites (1998).

nodes.label: Martyrs of Amorion
nodes.full: Forty-two officers and officials, taken to Samarra after the fall of Amorion and held there for seven years, were executed on 6 March 845 for refusing to convert to Islam, according to the Byzantine hagiographical accounts, which went through several versions; the Arab sources do not mention them, and the cult became the focus of an official memory of Amorion.
nodes.src: Acts of the Forty-Two Martyrs of Amorion; Vasiliev 1935; Treadgold 1988.

nodes.label: The last Roman–Persian war
nodes.full: Heraclius’s victory over Khusrau II in 627–628 ended the long war of 602–628 and left both empires exhausted just before the Arab armies came.
nodes.src: background — see the Late Roman Anatolia folio (late-roman-anatolia-330-632)

nodes.label: The early Arab conquests
nodes.full: The Rashidun caliphate’s armies, after the Prophet’s death in 632, took the Persian empire and the Byzantine provinces of Syria, Palestine and Egypt within about twenty years.
nodes.src: background — see the Caliphate 632–750 folio (caliphate-632-750)
